title: Grant peace
hookLine: the Amidah ends asking for peace, goodness and blessing
last: NO ONE CAN SAY IT FOR YOU.

cards: So many things end on peace. Shalom is the word for hello and for goodbye. The Kaddish ends on it.
So does the priestly blessing from the book of Numbers.

Even the Mishnah, the great code of Jewish law, sixty-three tractates of rules about fields, festivals, courts and purity, closes its very last page with a sentence about peace. The Amidah follows the same pattern.
After praise, after thirteen requests, after thanks, the very last thing it asks for is shalom.

teach.h: THE PRIESTLY BLESSING: GIVE THEE PEACE.
teach.b: In the leader's morning repetition, just before this blessing, comes the priestly blessing. In the old Jewish translation, it ends: "The LORD lift up His countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."
In Israel, descendants of the priests, kohanim, come forward and say it every day; in many communities outside Israel, they do so on festivals.
Then the last blessing picks up the thread: Sim shalom. Grant peace, goodness and blessing, grace, kindness and compassion, to us and to all Your people Israel.

Bless us, our Father, all of us as one, with the light of Your face. Blessed are You, who blesses Your people Israel with peace. The light of Your face is borrowed straight from the priestly blessing.
All of us as one: peace is something no one can have alone.
Shalom comes from a root meaning whole, complete. It's not only the absence of fighting. It's nothing missing.
In many Ashkenazi communities, the afternoon and evening services use a shorter version, Shalom Rav, abundant peace. And that sentence on the Mishnah's last page?

teach.h: THE ONLY VESSEL THAT HOLDS BLESSING.
teach.b: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta says that God found no vessel that could hold blessing except peace, and quotes the Psalm: "the LORD will bless His people with peace."
A vessel: all the other blessings, health, livelihood, wisdom, leak out without it. So the Amidah puts the container last, to hold everything that came before.

how: Sim Shalom is the final blessing of the Amidah, following the priestly blessing in the morning repetition; many Ashkenazi communities say the shorter Shalom Rav at the afternoon and evening services.

games.q: Rabbi Shimon ben Halafta asks: what vessel can hold all of God's blessings for a people?
games.why: peace. on the Mishnah's last page he quotes the Psalm: the LORD will bless His people with peace.

practice: Picture someone whose life feels un-whole right now, someone grieving, someone in a fight, someone pulled in too many directions.
On each out-breath, send them one piece of what's missing: rest, calm, a quiet evening, a phone call that goes well.
If you pray, you can ask for their shalom; if it's someone you're in conflict with, notice whether you can wish it for them too.

wordCard.voice: Sim Shalom. Grant peace. The Amidah's final blessing: peace, goodness and blessing, for all of us as one.

orig.note: Hebrew: grant peace. shalom from sh-l-m, whole, complete.

carryVoice: Your line: it's nothing missing. Peace holds all the rest. That's five hundred ninety-four days.
